- [2023/05/25] George Lakoff's "Women, Fire, and Dangerous Things" (1987) challenged traditional views on linguistic categories by proposing that they are organized around prototypes rather than fixed features. (Lakoff, 1987, pp. 40-45)
- [2023/05/25] Lakoff's prototype theory offers a nuanced understanding of word meaning and category organization in lexical semantics, suggesting that meaning is dynamic and context-dependent. (Lakoff, 1987, pp. 46-47)
- [2023/05/25] Ronald Langacker’s "Foundations of Cognitive Grammar" (1987) introduced the idea that linguistic meaning arises from the interaction between linguistic forms and cognitive structures. (Langacker, 1987, pp. 10-14)
- [2023/05/25] Langacker's work emphasizes the role of mental imagery, attention, and construal in shaping linguistic meanings, providing a new perspective on lexical semantics. (Langacker, 1987, pp. 203-205)
- [2023/05/25] Lakoff’s analysis of the category "bird" revealed that some members are more prototypical than others, illustrating the dynamic nature of linguistic categories. (Lakoff, 1987, pp. 46-47)
- [2023/05/25] Langacker's cognitive grammar highlights how spatial expressions like "in" and "on" depend on specific cognitive construals for their meanings. (Langacker, 1987, pp. 203-205)
- [2023/05/25] The contributions of Lakoff and Langacker to cognitive semantics have enriched the study of lexical semantics by emphasizing mental representation and cognitive processes in shaping linguistic meaning.
